name: Urnes Stave Church
description: The oldest of Norway's surviving stave churches, standing at Urnes on the Sognefjord and dated to around 1130. Its carved west portal shows the Urnes style of interlaced beasts and snakes, a Viking-age ornament the church kept even as it was rebuilt in the mid-12th century. The building is a UNESCO World Heritage site and a key link between pagan Norse animal art and Christian church building.

name: Ulfberht Sword
description: A class of high-quality Viking-age swords bearing the +ULFBERHT+ mark, found in large numbers in Norwegian graves and hoards. Their high-carbon steel was far better than most contemporary iron, making them treasured war gear; some surviving marks are forgeries on poorer blades. The name is Frankish, showing the best Norse swords were trade goods from the Rhineland, buried beside their owners.

name: Ushabti Figurines
powers: Answer the summons to labor in the afterlife in place of the deceased.
description: Small mummiform figurines placed in Egyptian tombs to perform field labor for the dead in the afterlife, inscribed with spell 6 of the Book of the Dead, in which the figure answers 'here I am' when summoned to work. A single burial could hold several hundred, from a modest clay set to the 413 ushabtis of Tutankhamun. The name derives from the Egyptian word for 'answerer.'
source: Book of the Dead, spell 6; tomb assemblages

name: The Uraeus
powers: Spits fire against the king's enemies; guards the brow as the eye of Ra.
description: The rearing cobra worn on the brow of the pharaoh and of deities such as Ra, embodying the goddess Wadjet, protector of Lower Egypt. The uraeus spat fire at the king's foes and stood for the blazing eye that defended the sun god, and it was worn by kings and gods alike. Golden examples survive on royal diadems, most famously the cobra and vulture of Tutankhamun's gold mask.

name: Ulu
material: Blade of iron or slate with wood, bone or antler handle
powers: The all-purpose blade of the household and the camp.
description: The broad curved blade of the Inuit and other Arctic peoples, held by a short handle and used for skinning, cutting meat, scraping hides, and preparing food; the ulu is primarily a woman's knife and a symbol of her household. Its shape let pressure be applied with the whole arm, cutting through thick hide and frozen meat alike. Modern steel ulus are still made and used in the North today.
source: Inuit tradition and Arctic ethnographic records

name: Baganda Barkcloth (Olubugo)
material: Beaten inner bark of the mutuba fig tree
description: Olubugo is the barkcloth of the Baganda of Uganda, made by beating the inner bark of the mutuba (fig) tree into a soft, chestnut-brown textile. Men traditionally prepared the cloth, which was worn by kings and chiefs, used in burials, and remains a sacred material; UNESCO lists Baganda barkcloth-making as intangible cultural heritage.
source: Ganda barkcloth tradition; UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage
